source_refs.note: Book p. 27: 2.2 Finding the Intersecting Point(s) Graphically, the definition of a point of intersection (text before 2.2.1)

blocks.text: The point of intersection is a point where two or more graphs meet on the coordinate plane. This point represents the solution(s) to the equations of the given functions.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is a meeting point a solution? The graph of \(y = f(x)\) is the picture of every point \((x, y)\) that satisfies \(y = f(x)\). A point that lies on two graphs at the same time satisfies both equations at the same time, so its coordinates are a solution of the two equations together (a solution of the system).
So "solve graphically" means: draw both graphs on the same axes and read the coordinates of the point(s) where they meet.

blocks.title: Teaching note
Exam tip
blocks.text: A graph is read by eye, so the values may be approximate (for example 0.6 instead of \(3 - \sqrt{6}\)). Whenever you can, check a point read from the graph by substituting it into both equations: both must be satisfied.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Point of intersection = a point common to two or more graphs.
2. Its coordinates satisfy every one of the equations, so they are the solution(s) of the system.
3. Graphical method: draw all graphs on the same axes with the same scale, then read the meeting points.
4. Check the points you read by substitution.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Drawing the two graphs with different scales or on different axes: the meeting point is then meaningless.
2. Reading only the \(x\)-value: a point of intersection has two coordinates, \((x, y)\).
3. Trusting a rough sketch: plot several accurate points from a table of values.
